utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was not informed of any preliminaries. Yes, apparently there are preliminaries. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Two brief procedural or administrative matters, the first with respect to P1684, which is marked for identification, a translation, an English translation has now been uploaded into e-court. The Prosecution requests that it be attached to the B/C/S original and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is instructed to attach the English translation to P1684 and P1684 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, if there are any problems with the translation, you may revisit that within the next 48 hours. Next, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second issue, Your Honour, relates to two 92 bis motions, first, the 28th motion filed on the 23rd of May and the 29th motion filed on the 14th of June. Both time periods for response has expired. The Prosecution maintains its original position that it does not oppose any reasonable amount of time the Chamber deems necessary to answer those motions but would ask that they -- a definite date be fixed for a response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were kindly warned by my learned friend this morning about this issue so if we can answer tomorrow, because I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I. So you have until tomorrow, Mr. Lukic, to come up with a proposal for when, and then the Chamber will consider whether it accepts it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. We are ready to go with General Skrbic, though I would request a caution for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he will give his evidence viva voce?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, I thought that you asked for three hours, which is for a one-hour viva voce testimony rather long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is. We'll finish this witness today for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For sure, because usually for a viva voce witness, the same amount of time or even a little bit less is appropriate. So please keep that in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic. The rules require that you make a solemn declaration at the beginning of your testimony. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please be seated. Mr. Skrbic, you will first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. And you'll find him to your right. But before we do so, I'd like to inform you of the following. Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence state that a witness, that is you in this case, may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate yourself. We then could compel you to nevertheless answer the question, but any testimony compelled in this way, if it comes to that, shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you. One exception, if you would not testify in accordance with the truth, then that rule that it could not be held against you would not apply. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you completely, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. McCloskey will now start his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July 1995, can you tell us your position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The establishment position I occupied in July 1995 was called assistant commander at the Main Staff for organisational, mobilisation and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had recently been promoted to general that summer, had you not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: By virtue of a decree of the President of Republika Srpska, dated 24 June 1995, I was promoted into Major General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you're a career military officer that went through the ranks in the former JNA, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe briefly for us when you came over to the VRS and your positions leading up to your appointment as assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation and personnel with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I joined the Army of Republika Srpska on the 17th of December, 1993, and I was assigned to the position of assistant commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps of the VRS for morale, religious and legal affairs. I discharged those duties until 24th July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go 24 July 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of July, 1994, pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, I transferred to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to be able to briefly describe to us your position as assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation and personnel, but first, can you tell us of those three segments what you spent most of your time doing of those three? If, in fact, there was one.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the sector that I headed, most of the time was spent on personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief description of your job as assistant commander for personnel? What did you -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was not the only one who was handling these affairs. It was the entire sector that I headed, and the personnel affairs consisted of several important categories and these are: Education of officers and NCOs of the VRS; assigning officers and NCOs in the army as a whole; appointments of officers and NCOs; making proposals for promotion; and retirement of the officers of the VRS once they meet the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. Who did you make your proposals to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: With regard to all the affairs that I listed, I made proposals to my superior commander, the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe for us a little bit about your duties regarding mobilisation? Mobilisation of what, for example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian language, Your Honours, mobilisation has the meaning, which I believe we share with Mr. McCloskey, of appealing to civilians and businesses to provide assistance in terms of manpower and resources. So in that sense, I listed the needs of the Main Staff of the VRS in terms of mobilisation, manpower and material assets and made those proposals to the Secretariat for Defence of Republika Srpska, which was in charge of the mobilisation affairs that I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall in prior testimony describing your job as assistant commander and those of the other assistant commanders as the Main Staff as experts in the implementation of General Mladic's orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've already mentioned that you made proposals to General Mladic. Can you now just briefly tell us what you meant when you say that you and the other assistants were experts in the implementation of his orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there are two dimensions to the same process. First of all, we make proposals to the commander, for instance, me in my area, I make proposals regarding promotions, and then the commander decides whether to agree with my proposal or not. If he agrees, and gives a green light, then it is my responsibility to implement his order in practice, with my professional skills. We write appropriate enactments such as orders on promotion or we prepare decrees for the president of the republic to promote officers into the highest rank, which is general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go right to the 12 July 1995, which you have, as you know, discussed before. And did you get a call that day to do a particular -- to get a task going?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, Mr. McCloskey, that it was not on the 12th of July, if we mean the same task, the same issue. It was on the 11th. If you mean what you -- what I think you mean, namely mobilisation, because we discussed this issue for a long time. That was on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That wasn't a test. That was my mix-up. So the phone call that you've talked about many times, you received on the 11th of July. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, in the evening, or, rather, late at night, I received a telephone call, and the collocutor, whose name I still can't remember, informed me that buses need to be commandeered as soon as possible or mobilised as we say in Serbian. I passed on this demand also by telephone to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, and 10 to 15 minutes later, a person called Momcilo Kovacevic called me back. Momcilo Kovacevic told me, General, I understood your request but I kindly ask you to put this request in writing tomorrow so that we can implement what you requested on behalf of the Main Staff. And that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have in the past told us where this demand came from, have you not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That demand came from the operation centre located at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what person was behind that demand, as far as you knew? The demand for buses.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I know that very well. It was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to Exhibit 65 ter 04034. And as you just testified, you were asked to get that writing on paper. I'm sorry that this is not a great copy but they will blow it up for you. And we can see that this is from your sector dated 12 July to the RS Ministry of Defence, asking in the utmost urgency for at least 50 buses to be sent to Bratunac. Is this the written order you -- or the written document that you were just speaking of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04034 receives number P1710, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1710 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And sir, was it your understanding that the MOD understood that this was coming from someone besides just General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what was important there was the functional link. General Skrbic perhaps did not play the most important part there. But they know, you see the logo, Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. They know that it comes from the Main Staff and they took it very seriously, as an imperative. They could have disregarded it but, in that case, major complications would have resulted. So they understood this document as very urgent and that's the way they acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at the time, did you know what these buses were to be used for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was told that the buses were needed for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what else did you know about evacuation, for who and from where, if you know, or if you were told at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, everything is defined in the last sentence of this document. If you need me to, I can read from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I want to know at the time, on the 11th and 12th of July, did you know who was going to be used -- who was going to be evacuated in these buses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know where these unknown persons were going to be evacuated to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I didn't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At some point, did you find out who was evacuated and where they were evacuated to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That was 20-plus years later. Judges, Your Honours, I studied a series of documents and now I know what those buses were used for. Your question was did I know at that point in time, and I answered no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you know what these buses were used for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many days later, but when I saw on television, I don't know which studio it was, maybe Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republika Srpska, I heard that those buses had been used for the evacuation of women and children. Later on, I found out that this video report was made by a journalist called -- I can't remember his name now, it doesn't matter -- who filmed it also for the Radio Television Serbia. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you learn from information from the VRS or the Main Staff how these buses you helped mobilise were used?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More than a week after the 12th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. McCloskey, that it was around the 18th or the 19th July, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to some of the other documents you've seen before. Let's start with Exhibit 65 ter 04008. And we'll recall that your document was to the MOD, and as this comes up, we'll see that this is from the Secretariat of the Defence Ministry of Sarajevo, and it refers to a request from the Main Staff and it gives that number, and I think everyone will agree that that's the same number of your previous order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this MOD document, is that a result of the -- your document that we saw before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when, to your knowledge, were any buses from Sarajevo, the Sarajevo area, when were those buses returned to the Sarajevo area of Republika Srpska after their use here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if prisoners were used -- were put in those buses and transported from the Srebrenica area to the Sarajevo area, who would be responsible for monitoring the movement of those prisoners from the Drina Corps area to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps area? This is something that you did answer before.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It wasn't only in terms of these buses but all buses used to that end. In that respect, it was the task of the civilian traffic police and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall telling us it was the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall having told you that it was the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I do. Possibly parts of the military police of the Drina Corps were engaged as well, but I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment was Colonel Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was his commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: His commander was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I would offer this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04008 receives number P1711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1711 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 65 ter 04010?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, we can see this is a similar document, just this time from Zvornik. So is this like the other one, this came from your order as we see the number down in this doc?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, that is the case. I do have to point out an imprecision here. At the top of the document, just before the number 02-21 and so on, it should also include the heading of the Ministry of Defence of the RS. It should be just before the confidential number 02-21. It was the minister of defence sending this document to the Secretariat of the Defence Ministry in Zvornik, that sent it. The next indication is the signature. In the signature block we see Assistant Minister Momcilo Kovacevic who is the same person we mentioned appearing on the previous document. Let me conclude in a single sentence, then. This document, which is authentic, was sent by the Ministry of Defence of the RS to the Secretariat of the Defence Ministry in Zvornik. The contents are authentic the way you quoted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put just one question for clarification, Mr. Skrbic? You referred to the name of the person Momcilo Kovacevic but can you recognise the signature in the original? Is that the signature of Mr. Kovacevic or did somebody else sign on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, this is not Momcilo Kovacevic's signature. He was the assistant minister. Banduka signed in his stead. I know him as well. I would like to draw your attention to the small line -- yes, I see it in English, it says "for." In other words, Mr. Banduka signed for the assistant minister, Momcilo Kovacevic. And we see here R Banduka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's Mr. Banduka's first name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as for the first name of this man, Banduka, I can't recall it, but he's definitely not Rajko Banduka because Rajko Banduka was not with the Ministry of Defence. He was with the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, Rajko Banduka of the Main Staff, what was his job?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Rajko Banduka had the duty of adjutant of the Main Staff commander, General Mladic. Later on, in late 1995, we transferred him to another duty in the office of the Main Staff commander. However, he continued exercising the duty of adjutant to the commander of the Main Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was General Mladic's nickname for him? If there was one.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, he did not have a nickname. We all called him Rajko. That was his first name, not his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04010 receives number P1712, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1712 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have Exhibit 65 ter 25812.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm switching topics now, General. This is a document I know you've seen before. It's a Drina Corps document which, as we can see, it's 13 July, from the chief of personnel of the Drina Corps, entitled: "The transfer of duties of corps commander." And we can see that it's from Zivanovic to General Krstic. Did this in fact happen as noted in this document, as far as you know, a transfer of command from Zivanovic to Krstic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a handover of duty, as stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you meet President Karadzic on the 14th of July, the next day from this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I don't quite understand why you make this link with the 13th. I was unaware of this document until I testified in the Karadzic case, I think. It is when I realised that this document was drafted before I went to see Mr. Karadzic, the president of the republic, on the 14th of July, 1995, in order to have a decree issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my point. So when you saw President Karadzic on the 14th, did you have anything to do with this -- the promotion of General Krstic? Can you tell us what a decree is, in that regard?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you were probably mistaken in saying that General Krstic was promoted. He had been promoted previously. The decree had been prepared for the president to sign. The contents were as followed: General Krstic is being appointed to the duty of commander of the Drina Corps. Colonel Svetozar Andric is to be appointed the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So my point is, just briefly, that the Main Staff was aware of this promotion and you worked with President Karadzic to get it done correctly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff was aware, but it did not occur through standard procedure, that is to say, during a meeting of the collegium of commanders of the Main Staff -- from the Main Staff. The proposal came from the commander of the VRS Main Staff. When he told me to draft a decree to be taken to the president, I could have told him, "General, sir, did you have a good think about this?" But there was no reason for me to do so. So I carried the decrees to the president and he signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were when General Mladic told you this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was always at the rear command post in Han Pijesak. Apologies, Your Honour. It's a problematic area but in any case, at the time, I was in Han Pijesak, at the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber has heard about the command post at Crna Rijeka, and can you tell us very briefly about this command post, the rear one, in the town of Han Pijesak itself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I will try to be brief in answering your question precisely, because you seem to have mixed up some things. I apologise for that. The basic command post of the Main Staff was in Crna Rijeka. The rear command post of the Main Staff was in Han Pijesak. These two locations are between three and five kilometres apart, although I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, one of your previous questions was whether the witness remembers where he was "when General Mladic told you this." He told us where he was, but he has not confirmed that it was there that General Mladic told him, by the way, what exactly. Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, can you tell us where General Mladic was when he told you about the promotion of Krstic, where you were, and what General Mladic said, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to apologise for this half question, if I can put it that way. I understand Mr. McCloskey when he says "promotion." In his mind it is someone being promoted to a higher position, but in my parlance, it is simply promotion in terms of rank. There is always this distinction in my mind. Krstic was not promoted to a higher rank in the course of those few days. He was promoted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. The issue is where Mr. Mladic was when he told you about the new position of General Krstic. And did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember where he was, Your Honour, whether at Crna Rijeka or somewhere else but I do know he told me so. It is also possible that he told me that over the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25812 receives number P1713, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1713 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, to switch to another topic, in the Popovic case you told us that Colonel Milos Djurdjic was an aide de camp to General Mladic, is that correct? In the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I don't think I said so. Milos Djurdjic was never aide de camp to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into another subject, then. Do you recall going to a new year's celebration for the new year of 1996 with members of the Main Staff, including General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I know you've seen this before but I'd like to show you a short clip of a speech General Mladic gave there. It should be on P1147, and V009268. And it is starting at 21.53.1, and I hope to show you just a part where General Mladic talks about his core people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have not been provided with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can merely read out the subtitles. "Ladies, dear guests, colleagues, officers, and generals" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, if we can just let the interpreters rest and just read the subtitles ourselves, I think that was our policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think that was an agreement about subtitles, at least that the Chamber allowed them to be part of the exhibit. Could we then restart and the only thing, Mr. McCloskey, if it is not read, then of course, even if they are accurate, they are missing on the transcript for those who would read them after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is part of the trial video and the transcript, the agreed upon transcript, is now -- is in the record, the full transcript of this so we should be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can proceed, and the interpreters do not have to interpret the text. Could we restart?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we -- Ms. Stewart can go right to the key part so we should hopefully be able to finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we are starting at the key part, 23.53.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and we're stopping at 24.51.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you -- having lived this, do you agree with General Mladic of the people he named as his core people, as the people that made the decisions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: One may conclude so on the basis of General Mladic's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was: You lived it. Do you agree with General Mladic's assessment or was he embellishing a bit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It was a celebration, so he did embellish it a bit. However, the gist of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he spoke briefly about General Tolimir. Where did General Tolimir fit in, as far as you know, in the trust of General Mladic or lack thereof?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I rely on General Mladic's definition. In other words, he was a part of the inner circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall telling us at the Tolimir trial that he was one of the most trusted people of General Mladic's?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, thank you again for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think the wisest thing to do now would be to take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Skrbic, and we would like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, you may start your cross-examination. Mr. Skrbic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to inform you that I cut short my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask whether the next witness is ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I know that Mr. Vanderpuye is speaking with him right now for the first time. He just got in from the States so that would be a tough move. I've not spoken to Mr. Vanderpuye yet, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps he could organise it in such a way that we go over the simple matters first and -- of course, the problem is that he couldn't speak with him anymore once we have started hearing his testimony. We'll see how it develops. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that I am Branko Lukic and that I am on the Defence team of General Mladic. When you came to the Main Staff of the VRS, did anyone tell you that the second part of the command post of the Main Staff of the VRS was in the vicinity of the main command post but because it was attacked in 1992 by Muslim forces from Zepa, it was moved to Han Pijesak and that's why you were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I was aware of that even before I came to the Main Staff, because when I went to join the Army of Republika Srpska, I went via Han Pijesak, and from then on to Drvar. At Han Pijesak an officer, I can't remember who exactly, told me exactly what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move from subject to subject quickly only in the beginning. Today you've spoken about the Secretariat of the Ministry of Defence. Is that a civilian or a military body in the system of Republika Srpska in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Secretariats of the MOD all over Republika Srpska belonged to the Ministry of Defence. The Ministry of Defence is a ministry, an organ, of the government of Republika Srpska, and that's a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have been shown P1712.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to see it again in e-court briefly. I obviously wrote down the wrong number. This is not the document we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But even without the document I can ask you my question. R Banduka was mentioned in one of the documents. Do you know that at that time Rajko Banduka, ADC to General Mladic, was at the military medical academy in Belgrade undergoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move to some general issues now to provide a broader context for what I want to ask you. Is it true that in Republika Srpska, general mobilisation was never declared during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The process of general mobilisation is linked to the category of the state of war. The state of war was not proclaimed in the entire territory of the republic until some date in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, you said 20-something October, or perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the 20th or the 27th of October. I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war, right? At the time when Republika Srpska was losing a lot of territory in the west?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Because the war ended on 14 December 1995, after the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers? You asked whether in Republika Srpska general mobilisation was never declared during the war in Bosnia. Witness, you answered by saying that general mobilisation is linked to the state of war and you said that was never proclaimed, which does not yet answer the question about the mobilisation, or did you say there was no state of war, therefore there was no mobilisation at all, or was there a 99 per cent mobilisation? Or could you clarify what the consequences were of no state of war having been declared? And in factual terms rather than in theory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were partial mobilisations carried out by corps commands and other units, but there was no general mobilisation in Republika Srpska until October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, those partial mobilisations would be what percentage approximately of what would have been a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of percentage, it varied from 20 to 50 per cent. It was never 100 per cent mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, 20 to 50 and not being 100 is far away from each other. How many people who would be called upon by a general mobilisation were finally called upon by such partial mobilisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, all males between the ages of 18 to 60 were subject to military duty, and that means mobilisation. Republika Srpska had 370.000 men fit for military service. 370.000 were never mobilised because the army had, towards the end of the war, 209.000 members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is, therefore, on average well beyond 50 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the very beginning of the war, when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, it already had a certain amount of personnel. The reinforcement of the corps, the manning level, was between 70, 75 per cent. The least strong one was the one in Drvar Corps, and the highest manning levels was in the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and that was the only one that was manned to about 92 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking this question because when I asked you about the partial mobilisation, you said it varied between 20 and 50 per cent, then you gave a figure of 209.000 on a totality of 370.000 men fit for military service. And that is, therefore, well beyond 50 per cent and not anything between 20 and 50 per cent. Are you correcting yourself and say it was -- I mean, 50 per cent of 370.000 is 185.000 and there were far more than that so it was not between 20 and 50 per cent, if I follow you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, partial mobilisation lasted from 1992 until 1995. It was also done because we suffered losses and we had to summon new military conscripts to fill our units but we never achieved 100 per cent mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have already partially answered this question but I'd like to put it in a legal framework. Is it correct that the corps had the right to put requests to municipalities regarding mobilisation and reinforcement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is correct, except not to municipalities but secretariats of defence within municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Was work obligation under the competence of the army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned who was supposed to secure the convoys and, among others, you mentioned police forces, that is to say, not the military police but civilian. The police, together with the army, comprised the armed forces of the RS, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the law, police forces engaged in combat are under the command of the army? Under the law, in combat, that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: According to the law, when there is a state of war, then the police forces are commanded by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In practice, did it happen that police forces were under the command of the army, or did it not happen, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am unaware of such practice. As far as I was informed, in terms of combat, the police and army cooperated. They acted jointly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I would ask for another clarification. You just asked the witness, this is page 24, line 5 and 5 through 7: "You mentioned who were supposed to secure the convoys and, among others, you mentioned police forces, that is to say, not the military police but civilian." Earlier, the witness was, during examination-in-chief, asked about the buses, page 10, line 25 through page 11, line 2, he answered: "It wasn't only in terms of these buses but all buses used to that end. In that respect it was the task of the civilian traffic police and the military police." Therefore, I'm not quite sure if you are talking about the same matter raised during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not excluding military police. I just wanted to emphasise that he -- that the gentleman -- actually, general mentioned civilian police and that I was asking only about that segment. I'm not telling -- and I'm not challenging that there was military police in the same operation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier, in your previous testimony in other cases, you were asked about directive number 7 and the operation in Srebrenica. My question for you today is this: Was there any discussion at the Main Staff of the VRS concerning the planning of that operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. Where I was present, the planning of that operation was not discussed whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also attended collegium meetings, correct? Was it discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said no, it was not discussed at collegium meetings of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the Main Staff commander is not present, who acts on his behalf? I suppose you know that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As per establishment, it is so defined that the Chief of Staff is also deputy commander of the Main Staff. No particular documents are necessary to further regulate that situation. In other words, when the commander of the Main Staff is unable to attend to his tasks, he is replaced by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many deputies did the Main Staff commander have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Only one, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many assistants did he have?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff commander had six assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the role and position of General Milovanovic was different to the position of the six assistant Main Staff commanders [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I did not refer to General Milovanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Nicolai Milovanovic"] but General Manojlo Milovanovic was at that position. Irrespective of who the person is in that position, it is his duty to act as the deputy commander because that person's competence is defined by his establishment post. The person in that position during the war was General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a clarification and translation, it says assistant Main Staff commanders, and if -- that should be assistant commanders of the Main Staff, it's a significant difference. And also, there is a -- it's Nicolai Milovanovic. I think that will get corrected but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an obvious mistake there. But for the first one, Mr. Lukic, I don't know what language you used in your own -- in B/C/S but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, in terms of General Milovanovic, that -- the term I used is "deputy commander." As for the other six persons, the term is "assistant commanders."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you verify with the witness whether he understood the question in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand me when referring to General Milovanovic that I said he was a deputy Main Staff commander as opposed to the other six persons whom I termed assistants to the Main Staff commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The duty of General Manojlo Milovanovic was as follows: The Chief of Staff; at the same time deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Chief of Staff is not present, who decides on the person who is supposed to replace him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff decides that. If he's to be absent for objective reasons for a prolonged period, then he's replaced by the second officer in command. In other words, it is the commander of the Main Staff, and my sector drafts an order on that replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not everything was caught in interpretation. You said an order to act in his stead. Can you explain to us what it is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, by virtue of that document it is regulated for what period of time one person is to stand in for another. That role may not be longer than six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just get some clarification. Witness, at page 27, lines 17 to 20, you said in answer to the question who decides on the person who is supposed to replace the Chief of Staff, you said: "The Chief of Staff decides that. If he is not -- if he is to be absent for objective reasons for a prolonged period, then he's replaced by the second officer in command. In other words, it is the commander of the Main Staff ..." I thought the commander of the Main Staff would be -- would not be the second officer, would be the very first person. Isn't that so? The commander of the Main Staff would be Mr. Mladic but he's not the second officer. So when you say "the second officer in command ... in other words the commander of the Main Staff," I'm getting a bit lost. Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for confusing you. What I said was if someone else is supposed to stand in for the Chief of Staff, then it cannot be he who decides who will be standing in. That is decided on by the commander of the Main Staff. He defines the situation as follows. General Milovanovic will be substituted by General Miletic. It wasn't General Mladic who was supposed to soon in for another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it is also not the Chief of Staff who decides that. It is General Mladic who decides that, the commander of the Main Staff, who decides that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the clarification. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I will have to come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it needs to be decided who will stand in for the Chief of Staff, who will be the first person to do so? Is it the chief of the Main Staff or is it directly done by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I discuss facts here. It is a fact that no one ever stood in for Manojlo Milovanovic, because he was always in the territory controlled by the VRS. There is no order in existence on anyone standing in for General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified about the following. It is whether in practice you ever had an opportunity to find yourself in a situation where a document is signed by President Karadzic, the document that was supposed to be verified by the commander of the Main Staff, but that President Karadzic signed such a document even though it had not been reviewed by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, even with the greatest of efforts, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before you clarify your question, you started by saying, "You testified about the following ..." Were you referring to previous testimony or were you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think for the Chamber to be able to follow the question, it would be good --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what the testimony at that point in time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was not clear enough and I will correct myself. I would like to call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic apparently wants to consult with counsel and he can do so but at non-audible volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed. [Interpretation] I don't see the 65 ter number now. I'll find it hopefully in another place. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need your testimony of 17 September 2007, which was a Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe 29059.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why we don't have it. That's right, 29059, that's why I was confused. And we need e-court page 62, which should correspond to transcript page 15523. And I will read from lines 18 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, first of all, let me tell you that this was a discussion about directive number 7, signed by the president, and I will now quote the question. [In English] "Q. And who is able to make corrections and return the directive? "A. Well, I suppose that the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS had to review this document before the president signed it, but sometimes the president signed even though the commander of the Main Staff wasn't aware of it, and I don't know whether the commander of the Main Staff reviewed this or not." [Interpretation] So my previous question, which may have been confusing when I put it first, was, did you know of cases when President Karadzic signed documents that should have been previously reviewed by the commander of the Main Staff but had not been?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. I was not aware of that, but I stand by my statement, my evidence that I had given and you had just read in the English language, and I would not change anything to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 65 ter 14580?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, this document has been shown to you before, and I will not go into the detail that my colleagues at previous trials had gone into, but it's a letter by President Karadzic that he sent to General Milan Gvero, late Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no English translation of this document. Actually there is but there is no document under it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- this number. [Interpretation] I will just read out briefly and we won't go into the essence of the document. I'm just showing you a document from which we see that President Karadzic contacted General Gvero directly in his letter of 18 December 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we nevertheless see it on our screens, even if it's only English version? Oh, let me see. Yes. Oh, it's -- I'm a bit confused by your observation, Madam Registrar, that an English document is there but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is only B/C/S version and there is something uploaded as English translation but it's empty page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will correct it and I will not deal with that substance of this document at all at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you started already by asking a question. But let's proceed for this moment, and if the Prosecution would know of an English translation which can be produced quickly - I see Ms. Stewart is working hard - then that would be highly appreciated. It is a document apparently of the 18th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just informed that we have the translation after 1D1 -- 1104, 1D1104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that President Karadzic was able to contact anyone on the Main Staff or any of the corps, as Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not only was he able to, but we see that he did it in practice. That is not forbidden him anywhere in so many words. The president can contact a soldier if he wants to, but to leave a trace of bypassing the commander of the Main Staff and addressing an assistant commander of the Main Staff of the commander is contrary to the system of competences, the hierarchy. General Gvero should have informed General Mladic that he received this document. In some previous trials, some evidence was shown to me that General Gvero did that, but he still answered this letter, I suppose with the approval of the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's very difficult to understand both the testimony and the document if we do not know what happened before this letter was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll try to clarify them a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it true that the relations between President Karadzic and General Mladic, as well as the relations between President Karadzic and General Gvero, at the moment of writing of this letter were disrupted to a great extent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They were disrupted, especially between General Gvero and the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that President Karadzic had asked for the dismissal of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct, more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that President Karadzic also wanted General Tolimir replaced, as well as Djukic, Lisica, Milutinovic, and even General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you enumerated a lot of them. There was a particular situation for each of these generals. MPs in the Assembly of Republika Srpska asked for the replacement of Djukic, Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic, General Gvero, but not General Ratko Mladic. However, the president of the republic tried to replace General Ratko Mladic already back in 1993. I wasn't there at the time but I heard that story. And then he moved him to a different duty, which was advisor for defence at the Office of the President of the Republic. Since that duty did not exist according to establishment, we in the Main Staff understood that he simply replaced General Mladic. The president did not write a decree replacing any of these generals and putting them on stand-by, but he spread the story around his party and in his entourage that these generals need to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in this respect. Whose competence was it to appoint or to replace a general? Was that not the competence of the Supreme Commander, being the President of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. That was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you say that President Karadzic wanted to get rid of many of these generals at one point in time, he could have just have signed a decree saying that you are hereby dismissed from your function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, but he did not do that. He did not issue a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, he apparently was not determined to -- no speaking at a level which can be understood by anyone else in this courtroom. I started my question. I said, apparently he was not determined to dismiss them because, otherwise, he would have signed a decree to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just consult briefly with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and would you please tell him that he should keep his volume down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a time frame, especially for that last attempt, as he says, to fire Mladic? The time frame is key to all these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, Witness, when it was you said that Mr. Karadzic wanted to have Mr. Mladic to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard the story that he wanted to replace him back in 1993, but I know for a fact that the president wrote a decree replacing General Ratko Mladic on the 4th of August, 1995, and appointing him advisor for defence to the president at the military Office of the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But from whom did you learn that Mr. Karadzic wanted to replace General Mladic in 1993? Do you have any basis for what you heard, from whom did you hear it, why didn't it take effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from General Manojlo Milovanovic. He told me, Your Honours, that he did not want to accept that duty, and that's why, in the opinion of General Milovanovic, that replacement did not take effect. Those were the words of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who did not want to accept what duty, as you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Manojlo Milovanovic did not want to accept the duty of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know - and if you don't, simply tell us that you don't know - whether President Karadzic contacted General Krstic directly concerning the planning of the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that firsthand. I know that second hand, from the book of Dr. Kosta Cavoski where he cited an example where President Karadzic contacted General Krstic in Vlasenica and approved the Srebrenica operation. I don't know if I may tell you, Your Honours, that in my testimony in the Karadzic case, I confirmed that document because Mr. Karadzic showed me that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, books written by whomever who played a role, and I don't know who this author is, Dr. Kosta, but the Chamber usually has some hesitation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked if the general had his personal knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has no personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He has no personal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- he just read it in a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. When I say "please proceed," I'd forgotten to look at the clock. We will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have much after the break, how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes. Could we also hear after the break, Mr. McCloskey, what your plans are as far as the next witness is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, nothing as yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will hear from you after the break. The witness may be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, as far as the next witness is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've been trying to find Mr. Vanderpuye. He's working with the witness in some room, and someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw him in the corridor --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ah. Well, I hope he's [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's apparently not in a room but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. He should get my concern passing on your concern, and so we can hear back from him, but I didn't contact him. I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have asked him but I refrained from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we are nearing the end of this examination. I only have a few questions left. Let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1710 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the document, I can tell you it is your document with your typed signature of the 12th of July, 1995. From this document of yours, as well as other documents that were shown today by the Prosecution, which were sent by the Ministry of Defence or its secretariat, we see that buses were sent to Bratunac. At that moment in time, there was no one in Bratunac, out of the people that required transportation. Do you know who rerouted the buses from Bratunac to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that many documents regarding the commandeering of the buses remained. Did anyone ever tell you that it was supposed to be a covert operation, that it was supposed to be secret?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. No one ever told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said, "We can see that many documents regarding the commandeering of the buses remained." What did you refer to exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That still they are available for -- there are documents in regard of this mobilisation or commandeering of the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen until now three, isn't it, this morning? We saw the request for mobilising 50 buses. We see then an order to send at least 20 buses from several places. And then other buses to be sent by Zvornik, I think. Is that all you refer to or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are more documents, Drina Corps, there are documents also from the list of the Prosecution but since they did not use it, we do not intend to use those documents. Maybe that's why I was talking about many documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the reason is we -- you put to the witness that there are many documents remaining. I don't know whether the witness is aware of it and you have not been very specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not -- you could have asked that question without that introduction and then the answer still stands, I think, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm sure that the witness is aware of those documents since he testified about them in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this period, you went to Krajina, correct? When did you go there and why? Briefly tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Krajina, which is the western part of Republika Srpska, it is where I went in early August 1995. Some Main Staff officers had gone there even earlier, in late July that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Krajina, did you find General Mladic there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think it was at Kula. It is a location near Mrkonjic Grad. Mrkonjic Grad is between 70 and 80 kilometres away from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am asking you this concerning your statement whereby you say that at Main Staff collegium meetings there was no discussion of Srebrenica. From today's point of view, it sounds rather odd, probably from the point of view of the Chamber, and the Prosecution, and Defence. In order for us to understand, kindly describe to us what kind of situation you encountered in Krajina and what were you busy with there? In a few sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It was a difficult situation for the VRS, starting with August 1994. However, the situation became the most difficult in late July, and it lasted until the end of the war, that is to say, the 14th December 1995, when we were left completely isolated, meaning the VRS and Republika Srpska. We had to oppose the offensive of Croatian forces from Croatia which were in coalition with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and assisted by NATO aviation, in terms of full air support. They all attacked Republika Srpska, and that is when we started losing chunks of territory and the towns such as Glamoc, Drvar, Petrovac, Jajce, Kljuc, Sanski Most. There was a danger of losing Prijedor and Novi Grad. In addition, refugees presented a large problem. They had come from the territory of Croatia, as well as those refugees from all of the towns I mentioned, which were in Republika Srpska. In brief, the problem was in the refugees occupying all roads where the army could conduct manoeuvres. Thus, we were rendered incapable of manoeuvring our units in order to place them in a position to offer at least some kind of resistance. As you know, the problem was resolved in a very negative way for the VRS and Republika Srpska. In addition to the refugees, we had suffered a lot of casualties, in terms of manpower, and we lost equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness or Mr. Lukic, I fail to see the connection between what happened in the Krajina and not discussing the Srebrenica operation in the collegium. That's totally unclear to me. Could you further clarify or could you put more specific questions to the witness, Mr. Lukic? But if the witness is able to establish a link between the two, we would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question, Your Honour. May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the enormous problems and tasks that we had to deal with in the western part of the RS, we simply had no time to discuss Srebrenica. There was simply no time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there was no time, although it was an operation of considerable magnitude. Nevertheless, you find no time to discuss it? Or concentrated in that area rather than in the Krajina, but you were with your mind in the Krajina but the operation without any discussion was developing near Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the 20th of July, 1995, there was simply no time for us to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But perhaps prior to that date, before the operation started? During the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I did not attend such meetings where Srebrenica would be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it may well have been discussed in the collegium but in your absence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many collegium meetings you did not attend? Well, let's say from mid-June to mid-July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always attended such collegium meetings when promotions, appointments and deployment of officers was discussed, but at such meetings, Srebrenica was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Skrbic, is it correct, and to the best of your recollection, that in the Main Staff of the VRS, the operation in Srebrenica was not planned or discussed, prior to its implementation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: According to what I subsequently learned, that was a Drina Corps operation. It was not a Main Staff of the VRS operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is where I'd like to conclude. General, thank you for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. McCloskey to put some further questions to you, you said to your knowledge the operation in Srebrenica was not planned or discussed in the Main Staff, it was all the Drina Corps. Now, why did you then ask for 50 buses to be mobilised if it -- I do understand that this came directly from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not directly from the Main Staff, but the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic. I was aware that this order emanated from him. Those buses had never been planned in that operation. And subsequently, when I read some documents about Krivaja 95, I never found a reference to it. The buses were commandeered on the 12th of July 1995. They were not part of any plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they became part of a plan on the 11th of July, when you were asked, not by the Drina Corps but by the commander of the Main Staff, or at least within Main Staff circles, to provide such buses.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct. They became part of that plan. But it's also true that the Drina Corps issued an order, which hasn't been shown to you but I know it, stipulated that their own buses, buses that they owned, be used for that purpose. They were as per establishment part of the Drina Corps, these buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, through the Main Staff, at least another 50 buses were asked for, not by the Drina Corps but through the Main Staff. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The Main Staff did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you asked for those buses and they should go to the Bratunac sports stadium. Did you have any idea what would happen when those buses would have arrived at the Bratunac sports stadium?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you sent buses to a certain place and then without any knowledge as whether they would stand there for 14 days waiting for further instructions by whomever?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It is not I who sent them. The Ministry of Defence sent them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked that they would be sent to the Bratunac sports stadium, and that is exactly what the minister of defence then told them to do. What, again, would, in view of you, happen when they arrived there? Who would receive them? Who would give further instructions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know who received, them but somebody was probably in charge of receiving them and telling them what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you sent -- ask you for 50 buses to be sent without any knowledge on who would receive them and tell them what to do, so if no one would have been there, the buses would have stood there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was not my responsibility to direct the buses. That was the job of the traffic police and the military police. They directed the buses. My competence ceased after writing the request to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I understood your evidence to be that the police would escort the buses. Now, if you are escorting a convoy of buses, someone must have decided on where they should be escorted to, or was it the military police who knew where they had to go and what to do, whom to load?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They knew on which road the buses should drive, and they took them - I suppose they took them - to the stadium at Bratunac. The military police had the responsibility to provide safe passage for the buses because there was the danger they might be attacked by Muslim forces, and the traffic police directed them along which route to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the traffic police tell them where to go? Would that be a decision for the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. The traffic police only received a route in order to be able to guide them in cooperation with the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom would they receive the route?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you asked for sending 50 buses without knowing in any way what they would be used for, where to go, who would give the instructions; the only thing you would know is that the police would escort for safety purposes? That's why you were asking 50 buses for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Up to the stadium in Bratunac, I said clearly in my request to the ministry, and they knew where this route leads. From Sarajevo, Zvornik, Bijeljina, they sent buses to the stadium at Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not interested that much in the route from Sarajevo to Bratunac but in any route on from Bratunac. Who would tell them where to go, who would tell them to go to Potocari and either to load men -- women and children or to load military-able men?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That sounds rather naive. Would you agree with me that asking for 50 buses, not knowing anything further, may sound a bit naive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It may sound naive to you, Your Honour, but I didn't have that problem. What mattered to me was the location where the buses should arrive, and that was enough. I suppose somebody must have been there to tell them what to do. Now, who told them, I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if not, you would have ordered 50 buses for nothing. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: 50 buses for nothing was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
