utterances.text: Well, you didn't know by whom they were received and what further instructions would be given. You had no clue. So if no one would have been there, the buses would have been gone there for nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: If you assume that, then they would have gone there for nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to assume anything else apart from a vague kind of someone will be there, someone will give instructions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The formulation that I put in the document was enough for me, namely, evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does it say "evacuation" in the document? It doesn't say anything about evacuation, does it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why didn't you write the purpose in the letter?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember why I didn't put it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Evacuation from whom, from where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: We often used buses to transport the personnel of the VRS, and we also used buses to transport population. Now, I learned later what these particular buses were used for, but at that moment, I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it was your special task to figure out how much mobilisation you would need, 50 buses equals 2500 people, approximately? 50 persons on a bus?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was not my job to make estimates, how many buses need to be commandeered. I was told that exactly 50 buses were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom was this told to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The officer who told me, over the phone, the task issued by the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you possibly consider 2500 of your own men to have to be transported at that point in time at that place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you earlier said about transportation of troops, for which you might need buses, that certainly would not apply, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So by 11 July, it was clear that approximately 2.500 people had to be transported, when you received that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What is the question? I didn't understand. It's true that I got that telephone call on the 11 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So by the 11th of July, the need for the transportation of approximately 2500 people was known within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The number was not mentioned, only the number of buses was mentioned, 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could that mean anything else than 50 times -- well, 45 or 50? Isn't it true that approximately 50 persons fit into a bus?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: How much would that be? I would need to do the sums. You said correctly, 2.500 people can fit in, but I didn't do the math. An infantry brigade numbers 2500 people. A Light Infantry Brigade is 1500 people. There were several brigades there from the Drina Corps. That could have occurred to me as an estimate, but I did not go into estimating why these buses were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A minute ago, you told me that it was inconceivable at that point in time that you would need transportation for 2.500 troops. So therefore I do not understand why you're now referring to troops, when you said that was not a possibility at that time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Only now did it occur to me how many men make an infantry brigade, and that's why I told you that, so you have an idea how many men an infantry brigade has. An infantry brigade has 2500 men. The 1st Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. There you told us a minute ago that it was not troops or brigades that had to be transported. So therefore the comparison is useless. I'm talking about 2500 persons. At this moment, I have no further questions for you. Mr. McCloskey, any -- yes, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just on the same topic. During the examination by the Presiding Judge, you used the term "evacuation" and then were you surprised that this term doesn't appear in your request signed by you of the 12th of July, 1995. Earlier this morning, you used the term "evacuation" as well. That is on page 9 at the end, just a moment, page 8, last line, you were asked by Mr. McCloskey: "And at the time, did you know what these buses were to be used for?" Your answer was: "I was told that the buses were needed for evacuation." That was your first answer. Then you gave different answers, that you -- some days later -- learned that they were used for transportation of women and children. And then you referred to studies of documents some 20 years later. You were told the purpose of requesting 50 buses were for evacuation. That was your first answer this morning. What kind of evacuation did have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Evacuation implies an evacuation of the population. That's what I had in mind, and I stand by the term "evacuation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have information that the population was gathered at the football stadium at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you specifically asked for 50 buses to be sent to the sports stadium in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to Mr. McCloskey, one other question is why would the civilian population, the women and the children, why would they have to be evacuated? They were living there. What was the military need to evacuate them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, beginning with 1992, and until the end of 1995, there were movements of populations throughout the Republika Srpska. Every part of the territory affected by combat saw its population evacuated. Only refugees from Croatia and the western part of Bosnia, or, rather, Republika Srpska, did not use buses. Instead they used tractors, trucks, horse-drawn carts, et cetera. They even walked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So was it intended, then, that the civilian population would move out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't know about intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why request 50 buses to be mobilised if there is no intention to evacuate, as you said, the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not the women and children. Evacuation, full stop. It's possible to evacuate population regardless of nationality, ethnicity. The Serbian population could be evacuated on these buses too because there was combat around. The population of my native place, Glamoc, fled. Nobody evacuated them. They went, escaped in a totally disorganised way, ran to forests. They fled before NATO bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber received evidence that the population of the enclaves at that point in time was, if not exclusively, almost exclusively non-Serb. So therefore my question then again is: You more or less implied as a suggestion that it could be Serbs to be evacuated, but the civilian population in that area to be evacuated apparently were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, sir. No, Your Honour. I didn't say Serbs. I said Serbs too could be evacuated. Kravica, Skelani, et cetera. Many other places around populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the 50 buses were needed not to evacuate the civilian population or whatever other population from the enclaves, but that they were requested in order to evacuate the Serbs from surrounding villages from Srebrenica? Is that what you're suggesting in your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's not what I'm suggesting. I'm just saying there was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there were almost no Serbs living in the enclaves, so if it's not the people around the enclaves, you said, well, also Serbs, but there were hardly, if any, any Serbs in the enclaves. At least that is evidence. The Chamber has not determined that, but until now the evidence suggests strongly that there were hardly any Serbs in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you're quite right. According to the census, from 1991, in Srebrenica there were 1400 Serbs as opposed to 3.400 Muslims and 146 Croats. Now, those 1400 Serbs, I really don't know where they are. They were not in Srebrenica because Srebrenica had been cleansed from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so there were no Serbs to be evacuated, if I understand your testimony well, from the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct, Your Honour, there were none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in the Main Staff, there were -- there was an awareness of a need for 50 buses for evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we see this document. It also says that the buses need to be sent to Bratunac by a certain time, they thought it was 1430 hours, on the 12th. So if those buses don't get to the stadium by the 12th or to Bratunac, the call would be to you, where were they, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That was not my responsibility. I would have probably, because you are also talking in assumptions, I would have probably received a new request to commandeer buses if those buses did not arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- you've also spoken of the Drina Corps and the Drina Corps getting their own buses and so I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that this is from the command of the Drina Corps on 12 July, and the stamp we see 12 July at 1000 hours on one of the segments. And we see that it's to the VRS Main Staff, command post. We know where that is. We also see to the rear command post for information. That's where you are, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, that's where I was, at the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had the responsibility to implement General Mladic's orders for buses, correct, see to it that it was implemented?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The person at the Ministry of Defence, as you've seen in some documents, Mr. McCloskey, made secretariats responsible for informing them immediately about the execution of their task, and as a good colleague, that person called me and said, "General, the buses had been mobilised."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were monitoring and -- Mladic's order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's right. Up until the moment of commandeering. That is when my task ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that it says, pursuant to the VRS GS commander's order to provide 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, and then they ask for fuel. So is this -- this is Mladic again, same order for 50 buses, or a different one, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say what kind of order it is, whether it was oral or written. It just says pursuant to the order. It means that the Drina Corps command and the commander were familiar with General Mladic issuing such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's all connected, Mr. McCloskey. Buses need fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's all connected. Could -- I would offer this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04143 receives number P1714, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I won't go into this. You've just referred briefly to the Serbs being run out of Knin, Glamoc, Grahovo, and I think you've said previously that that was a crime. Are you having trouble acknowledging you were involved in the bussing of the Muslims out of Srebrenica because you know that was a crime as well? You have the right to remain silent.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to remain silent in terms of this question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, the witness has no right to remain silent but can he invoke his right not incriminate himself which is not exactly the same, but the Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not compel to you answer the question. Please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would not insist and I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have a brief one on this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have before us the document. In the penultimate paragraph we find the following wording: Their final destination is unknown to us for the moment. Do you know who determined, since obviously the Drina Corps command on 12 July 1995 did not know what the destination was of these buses, do you know now, or did you know then, what the destination was? And do you know who had the right to decide on the final destination of these buses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It's misstatement of the evidence except for the last part. It's not the destination. The destination is clear, to Srebrenica, but what is not clear yet is the final destination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I took it that Mr. Lukic referred to the final destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Witness, where the command of the Drina Corps did not know what the final destination of these buses was, did you know at the time what the destination was or who could decide on what the final destination would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I knew that the buses were supposed to be in Bratunac at a particular time. As for the final destination, I was unaware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you know who could decide on the final destination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who would it be that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The VRS Main Staff commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you saying today that the Drina Corps commander could not decide on the destination of these buses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not without the approval by the Main Staff commander. It is my assumption, in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that is your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions for you, Mr. Skrbic. Therefore, this concludes your evidence in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have received word from Mr. Vanderpuye, and he is currently in the process of typing up a proofing note from the witness and really needs a bit of time to do that. And so we really can't bring him on today, time wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would not be good, Mr. Lukic, because you would not be aware of the content of the proofing note. You would have no time to consider it. Therefore I suggest that at the end of this session, that we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Suggestion accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we'll not adjourn until -- well, Mr. Groome most likely will read the transcript anyhow. We would like to enquire with the Prosecution about the remainder of the Prosecution's presentation of evidence and we do not expect an answer within the next few minutes, Mr. McCloskey. The Prosecution has repeatedly stated that its presentation of evidence may conclude in the fall of 2013. The Chamber has three inquiries in relation to that. Number 1: The Chamber would like to inquire whether it would be possible for the Prosecution to file all remaining Rule 92 bis, Rule 92 quater and bar table motions by the 30th of August, 2013. May I take it that you have no immediate answer to that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know internally we are trying to do that ourselves but as for committing us, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We would like then to hear from you or Mr. Groome in, well, let's say, within the next one or two days. Second: Could the Prosecution indicate the scope of what is still left to be tendered, for example, number of 92 bis, quater, witnesses, number of bar table documents? The Chamber would like have an impression on what we still can expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's known. That's just a matter of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we would like to hear from the Prosecution also within the next few days. Three: Could the Prosecution indicate where it stands in relation to tendering voluminous expert reports such as the one of Mr. Theunens, if you still intend to call Mr. Theunens, because the Chamber would then like to set a deadline for that. And we are thinking of the 26th of July. Because Mr. Theunens at present is scheduled to be called to testify mid-September. Then for other expert reports such as the ones for witnesses Tabeau, Treanor, and Brown, the Prosecution is also urged to file them as soon as possible. Mr. Groome will certainly read it and will discuss it with you, and we would like to receive answers to those inquiries within the few days to come. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 9th of July, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.12 p.m.,
